title: Rapid long-distance migration of RPA on single stranded DNA occurs through intersegmental transfer utilizing multivalent interactions
abstract: Abstract Replication Protein A (RPA) is a single stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding protein that coordinates diverse DNA metabolic processes including DNA replication, repair, and recombination. RPA is a heterotrimeric protein with six functional oligosaccharide/oligonucleotide (OB) domains and flexible linkers. Flexibility enables RPA to adopt multiple configurations and is thought to modulate its function. Here, using single molecule confocal fluorescence microscopy combined with optical tweezers and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations, we investigated the diffusional migration of single RPA molecules on ssDNA under tension. The diffusion coefficient D is the highest (20,000 nucleotides 2 /s) at 3 pN tension and in 100 mM KCl and markedly decreases when tension or salt concentration increases. We attribute the tension effect to intersegmental transfer which is hindered by DNA stretching and the salt effect to an increase in binding site size and interaction energy of RPA-ssDNA. Our integrative study allowed us to estimate the size and frequency of intersegmental transfer events that occur through transient bridging of distant sites on DNA by multiple binding sites on RPA. Interestingly, deletion of RPA trimeric core still allowed significant ssDNA binding although the reduced contact area made RPA 15-fold more mobile. Finally, we characterized the effect of RPA crowding on RPA migration. These findings reveal how the high affinity RPA-ssDNA interactions are remodeled to yield access, a key step in several DNA metabolic processes. Significance Replication Protein A (RPA) binds to the exposed single stranded DNA (ssDNA) during DNA metabolism. RPA dynamics are essential to reposition RPA on ssDNA and recruit downstream proteins at the bound site. Here in this work, we perform a detailed biophysical study on dynamics of yeast RPA on ssDNA. We show that RPA can diffuse on ssDNA and is affected by tension and salt. Our observations are best explained by the intersegmental transfer model where RPA can transiently bridge two distant DNA segments for its migration over long distances. We further dissect the contributions of the trimerization core of RPA and other adjacent RPA molecules on RPA migration. This study provides detailed experimental and computational insights into RPA dynamics on ssDNA.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This preprint has already left a small but meaningful downstream trace: it was later published in Journal of Molecular Biology, and it has one documented reuse in Europe PMC. The broader attention record is still sparse, with no citations recorded in OpenAlex yet, so the evidence currently points to early-stage scholarly uptake rather than established impact.

Full narrative

This study examines how replication protein A (RPA) moves along single-stranded DNA, addressing a basic question in DNA replication, repair, and recombination. Using single-molecule approaches, the authors focus on the role of RPA’s flexible, multivalent architecture and report rapid long-distance migration consistent with intersegmental transfer. The article sits at the intersection of biophysics, fluorescence methods, and DNA-protein interaction research, and its central contribution is a mechanistic explanation for how RPA may efficiently rearrange on ssDNA without losing overall engagement.

In terms of dissemination, the work began as a bioRxiv preprint and was subsequently published in Journal of Molecular Biology, indicating that it progressed from posted content into a peer-reviewed journal article. That publication pathway is the clearest signal of formal scholarly validation in the record. The article is also indexed in Europe PMC, where it appears as a downstream article mention, showing at least one documented reuse in a biomedical literature source.

The citation and public-attention profile is still modest. OpenAlex currently records zero citations, and the available discourse signals do not show broader online mention activity in the data provided. Rather than indicating lack of relevance, this more likely reflects a young publication with a record that is still accumulating. For a mechanistic, method-driven study like this, impact often emerges first through publication, indexing, and incorporation into subsequent biomedical literature before citation counts build.

Overall, the record shows a paper that has moved successfully from preprint to journal publication and has already been noticed in at least one downstream biomedical source. Its influence appears to be emerging through scholarly circulation rather than through large-scale public attention at this stage.
